en: Commentary on the Meaning of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra,
Section One: Explanations of Terms in the Commentary.
The ancient masters (and) the present school’s textual analysis (the ancient masters have two schools; the present school has four types of sections):

At that time, the four *siddhānta* interpretations explain the name and essence of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati as being empty, which applies throughout the latter three teachings (entrusted); their differences are as follows.
The meaning of the inexhaustibility of the three truths in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*);
the meaning of the inexhaustibility of the Middle Way within the ten inexhaustible dharma-gates of the *Avataṃsaka*;
and the meaning of the name of the Bodhisattva—[the latter] immediately rose from his seat, embodying the two cosmic principles.
He immediately rose from his seat and observed Śāriputra’s observance of the three truths;
he bared his right shoulder, following the ritual etiquette of foreign lands.

In this region, however, baring the shoulder is regarded as an act of arrogance—though there are exceptions, such as when Sūjia bared his flesh in apology or when Zhāng Yí did so out of necessity, yet it is not invariably considered a mark of pride.
Baring the right shoulder; the commentary on contemplating the mind; the commentary on the matter of joining the palms;
the contemplative interpretation that joining the palms symbolizes the revelation of the Real through the provisional;
and that joining the palms symbolizes the non-duality of the provisional and the real within the five aggregates.
Regarding the two interpretations of the question directed toward the Buddha, the answer possesses the two types of adornment.
Although there are many kinds of questions, the present inquiry is one that accords with the capacity of the audience.
By what causes and conditions is it explained in terms of the object, the wisdom, the capacity, and the response?
He liberates hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings; he relieves them from all sufferings and afflictions upon hearing the name of the Bodhisattva.
(Entrustment: Good and evil combined constitute the capacity [of the practitioner], perfected through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Single-mindedly invoking the Name has two aspects: the phenomenal and the noumenal.
Regarding the three teachings, they should not be simultaneous; yet in the Perfect Teaching, the response is simultaneous, and all attain liberation.
The word "all" (*jie*) reveals that the capacity of the sentient beings is universal, and thus the response is universal.
The meaning of enabling immeasurable capacities to attain liberation simultaneously is such that,
although the name has been invoked for many years, not an inch of benefit was received because it was chanted with a distracted mind;
therefore, through the sequential engagement of the three karmas, the vocal capacity attains liberation from the three kinds of suffering.
Within the removal of suffering, there is a small portion that bestows happiness;
within the bestowal of happiness, there is no removal of suffering, as it merely bestows the fruit of happiness rather than the cause of happiness.
Therefore, the ancient masters explained the seven calamities along with their origination.
There is a master who asserts that the wind-element of the feet constitutes one of the eight difficulties (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa).
Others have challenged this. According to the meaning of the sequence of the three karmas in our own school, the Sage should have no deliberation; in reality, there is no fixed sequence.
Our current interpretation holds that the sequence of the seven difficulties is merely cited as a representation of what is signified by those seven difficulties.

Regarding the seven difficulties, which are explained by way of what they represent as encompassing the three types of karma and the two factors of emptiness and consciousness that constitute the grounds for these difficulties, the explanation of each difficulty is presented according to three principles:
(1) a word-by-word commentary on the text; (2) citing concrete examples as evidence; and (3) an explanation through the lens of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Holding the two (the sixth being recitation and holding, while mental holding is maintained by the mind), as well as verbal holding, are all subsumed under vocal karma.

Whether it be "if there is," "furthermore there is," or "again there is," these are all indeterminate; the term "picking out" refers to escaping [the difficulty], while "holding" refers to encountering the difficulty, whether before or after.
The Tale of the Compassionate Maiden (Postscript): The Compassionate Maiden was a man;
Xie Fu of the Jin dynasty composed the *Yingyan zhuan* (Records of Verified Miracles), which Lu Guo of the Qi dynasty continued.
Four individuals who called her name were spared from the calamity of fire.

The *Huon guanxin shi* (Explanation of the Contemplation of the Mind through the Peril of Fire) states that there are three obstacles of fire, which correspond to the three contemplations. These include the fire of karmic retribution;
thus, the three paths—of segmented existence (*parīttābhava*), of skillful means (*upāya*), and of true retribution (*samyak-vipāka*)—each possess their respective fires.
The fire of karmic retribution extends from the hells up to the First Dhyāna;
[one] attains liberation from its characteristics. (Entrusted: The fire of anger and the fire of desire;
[one] attains liberation from their characteristics, as well as liberation from the fires of affliction.

The Bodhisattva is able to rescue through compassion; this does not depart from the two contemplations of Separate and Perfect, wherein the gradual contemplation consists of the three original vows of compassion that rescue one from the fires of the three obstructions.
[This concludes the section on] "White Bones and Flowing Light" (attached), as well as the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the ten bases of totality.
The three contemplations that rescue from the fires of the three obstacles;
the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) also simultaneously and universally responds through the *Huayan* fire-dharma gate (*huo-fa-men*). [Entrustment Note:
This is the aspect of the Perfect Contemplation and Compassion of the Separate Teaching Path rescuing one from the calamity of fire.
Rescuing from the Fires of the Three Obstacles:
Explaining the Meaning of the Twenty-Five Samādhis through the Narrowness of Other Interpretations; the Vast Function of the Twenty-Four Samādhis;
Part Two, the Water Calamity: Explaining the Reason for Being Drifted by the Great Flood.
The realization of the visualization for escaping the peril of water has three obstacles:
the water, the rākṣasa of craving and views, and the begging for a life-raft—the afflictions of the four flows.
(Postscript: Now, regarding ignorance (*avidyā*), it is distinguished from other delusions as being exceptional in its course.
The ability to observe both the general and the specific involves two intentions:
gradual observation and sudden response,
according to the Water Dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka* (as taught by the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha in the *Samantacakṣusūtra*).
Sudden Contemplation and Sudden Response:
Saving from the Waters of the Three Obstacles in Response to the Twenty-five Samādhis,

Third, following the section on the perils of the rākṣasīs, the number of people is explained;
it clarifies that while the winds encountered at sea are considered perils, they are not ultimate perils,
whereas the seven treasures are true treasures and the jewel is the supreme treasure.
Regarding the "black wind," others have explained it as the present moment; one person explains that by invoking the name [of Avalokiteśvara], all others are liberated.
Within this, the visualization of the name of Avalokiteśvara is established so that one may escape the perils of the *rākṣasa*. There are three types of obstructive winds (*vāyu*);

now, based on the wind, the visualization is set forth to explain the reason [for this liberation]. (A supplementary note. Now, the visualization is established in relation to the wind to explain the underlying principle.
The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*: Causes and Conditions; the Gradual and Sudden Contemplations;
the Gate of the Syllable *Vā*; Names and Meanings;
Saving from the Three Obstructions; and Correspondence with the Twenty-five Samādhis.

Regarding the fourth, the peril of weapons and staves: when weapons and staves strike and break one into pieces, one escapes the peril of weapons and staves through the direct realization of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*). There are three obstacles:
the rain falling from the Dragon King of Weapons and Staves, the six heavens, and the differing perceptions experienced by those who encounter them.
The afflictions are likened to swords and staves; the two contemplations—gradual and sudden—are able to respond to these swords and staves.
The letter *Dhā* (the gate of the letter *Dhā*) encompasses all that saves from the three obstacles;
the sword and staff correspond to the twenty-five samādhis in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Regarding the fifth, "the difficulty of ghosts":
the phrase "the three thousandfold world-system is filled" is a figurative expression.
Water and fire are not described as "filling" [the world-system] because, when contemplating and resolving [this matter], there are three obstacles regarding ghosts.
When the lust-demon and the anger-demon enter a person's mind, the three poisons manifest as these very demons;
their afflictions and karmas differ. (Furthermore,) moving karma and non-moving karma are such that the mind of views is the male demon, and the mind of desire is the female demon.
The gradual and sudden contemplations can respond to the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-gate for ghosts,
rescuing ghosts with the three obstructions through the twenty-five samādhis;
this is the sixth section, following the difficulty of shackles and fetters.
Regarding the presence or absence of offenses— including being bound by cangues, shackles, stocks, and fetters, or being exempt from them—
and the contemplation of manifest proof, there are three obstacles: shackles, fetters, wife,
children, wealth, and so forth, which are both retribution and karma.
The first three fruits [of the path] involve transgression, whereas the Arhat is without transgression;
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dapin) identifies those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as "Great Dragons" (*mahānāga*);
through both gradual and sudden contemplation, they are capable of responding appropriately.
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) constitute the three obstacles. (Appendix:
Regarding the Dharma-gate of Emptiness and Consciousness, both the four great elements and the seeds of emptiness and consciousness are empty.
One should contemplate the mind; for those whose faculties are not equal, one may sometimes observe external objects.
Regarding the seventh difficulty, that of hostile bandits: the root of enmity is the thief who seizes one's life;
the root of seeking wealth is the merchant leader and the merchants' precious treasures on a perilous road.
It is for this reason that one offers comfort, exhorts others, recites the name [of the Buddha], and praises his virtues.
Homage to the Sublime One.
Regarding the Contemplation of the Three Obstacles as Enemies and Robbers, there are the following sections:

the Merchant Master and the Merchants; the Precious Treasures and the Enemies and Robbers; the Covenant of Precepts; Listening to the Dharma; Cultivating Contemplation; and the Separate Explanations of the Primary and Auxiliary Practices.
The teacher and disciple, speaker and listener, both delight in the confusion of demonic principles and teachings; both lose [the truth].
Second, the second section clarifies the mental karma (*manas-karma*) and the three poisons:

the three poisons according to their capacity are explained as follows (a supplementary record): greed (*lobha*), anger (*dveṣa*), and hatred (*pratigha*)—these are single [factors]; lust, anger, and hatred, and ignorance (*moha*)—these are combined.
Desire, anger, and delusion lead to one’s own lust, hatred, and ignorance;
they cause others to break [the precepts]. It is said that those with little of these three poisons should contemplate Avalokiteśvara.
Whether the poisons are many or few, there are those who possess the capacity [to respond] and those who do not.
The Deep Characteristics of Women’s Lust (Entrustment Record): Zhou Bao appears to have many karmic conditions;
men and women with lust are afflicted by "lust-worms" and "lust-demons" that disturb their minds.
Whether one has much lust or little lust, the obstruction of the Path caused by anger is a grave matter.
The Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas (Appendix):
One should follow the example of the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* [in treating] lust, anger, and hatred; there are also demons and the afflictions of ignorance and delusion (and) there are demons.
[Appendix]: Separation from the three poisons; [Appendix]: The interpretations of others concern only suppression.

Now, explaining the scriptural text, we shall examine the six propositions concerning the contrast between partial and complete mindfulness and wisdom, which encompass the characteristics of penetrating and severing the notions of annihilation and permanence.
(Appendix: The present discussion shows that mindfulness is itself wisdom;
it points out the error of asserting that wisdom exists apart from mindfulness.
Constantly mindful of the characteristics of the cultivation of contemplation (entrustment): there are four propositions each for "forgetting" and "illumination" discussed separately;
regarding constant mindfulness, there are various four propositions based on the gradual and sudden approaches;
within each of the three contemplations, there are four propositions concerning "forgetting," "illumination," and their mutual transcendence.
Contemplative Understanding (Appendix): The Three Poisons Outside the Realm are Purified by the Name of the Heavenly Flower;

though the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the Two Vehicles remain unexhausted, the Three Poisons of the Bodhisattvas outside the realm disparage the Two Vehicles, like a great tree whose branches are broken off.
Beyond the realm of the three poisons, there are two types of Bodhisattvas who provide a counter-discourse on the contemplation of the three poisons (attached).
For ordinary people and Śrāvakas, the poison is slight; for those of perfect capacity, the poison is great.
(From the *Dapin wubushou*, Chapter 5).
The power of ignorance is great, yet the Buddha-wisdom can sever it;

even for a Bodhisattva, ignorance still possesses the three poisons, which serve as three gateways to the Dharma: (1) the gateway of grasping (greed), (2) the gateway of relinquishing (hatred), and (3) the gateway of neither grasping nor relinquishing (delusion).
Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion differ in essence from the compassion and loving-kindness found within the Four Immeasurables.

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) are like a great mass of fire that cannot be grasped from any side.
In the *Caryāgītikoṣa*, Mañjuśrī says: "I am desire, Śrī, and so forth. (Including the annotations: These are called "non-Buddhists" (*tīrthika*) and "perverse" (*mithyā*).
Regarding the three dharmas of seeing persons, there are two explanations concerning their engagement with conditions: the favorable and the unfavorable.
As for the woman Vāsudhārā, her lustful nature is both favorable and unfavorable.
To satisfy the King’s anger and his desires for both the favorable and the unfavorable,
he acted according to the Dharma: because actual harm is suffering,
he employed illusory means through both gradual and sudden contemplations to respond with compassion.

Clarifying the Body Action as the Catalyst (Part Two).
Regarding the reason why women seek to conceive a son as explained in the Sūtra: [First] the interpretation of others, [then] the present interpretation.
The Seven Failings of Women (Appendix): To be childless is the greatest suffering;
[therefore, one should pray for] the birth of a son endowed with merit and wisdom, or a daughter of upright appearance and auspicious marks, who shall be loved and respected by all.
Having planted the roots of virtue in past lives (entrusted),
one who has not planted wholesome roots in previous existences may,
through the karma of performing meritorious acts and prostrations during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), also escape calamities such as fire and water.

Citing the fulfillment of wishes through seeking, the evidence from the hells up to the heavens of desire shows that all possess the suffering of childlessness (Appendix Note). In the Avīci Hell, there is no thought of seeking children;
contemplate and understand how to seek sons and daughters.
In this Dharma-gate, ignorance is the father and craving and anxiety are the mother; the six sense-faculties are the sons and the six sense-objects are the daughters.
According to the external texts, heaven is yang and earth is yin, constituting male and female;
thus, by means of the supramundane Dharma-gate, it is explained that the parents give birth to their children.
Compassion is the female; the virtuous mind is the male. Samādhi is the female; contemplation is the male.
Perceiving the Buddha-nature in the Great Sūtra is the mark of a man.
Because these can represent the dharma-gate of "male" and "female"—which are difficult to represent—they are designated as male and female.
The four *siddhāntas* explain existence and non-existence through causes and conditions;
concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are non-dual yet dual, for concentration possesses wisdom and wisdom possesses concentration. (Entrustment: The text of this sutra is likewise;
by means of concentration and wisdom mutually possessing one another, it reveals that the essence is one.
The five precepts are correlated with the female of meditative concentration and the male of wisdom; the eight factors of the dhyāna branches are correlated with male and female;
the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the four immeasurables are specifically correlated with male and female;
and regarding the śrāvakas, one clarifies male and female in relation to the five methods of mental abiding as well as the contemplation of the principles of the Truths.
The three vehicles are illustrated by the analogy of the three beasts—the stag, the deer, and the elephant.
Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas, they are distinguished by their entry into and emergence from compassion and wisdom.

Regarding men and women, they are distinguished according to the *Tripiṭaka* (Three Baskets) Bodhisattvas. Regarding men and women, they are further distinguished according to the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).
According to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), the great compassion of male and female Bodhisattvas is clarified;
the name of the Grandmother of all Buddhas is "Great Woman" (Da-nü).
According to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), male and female [Bodhisattvas] and so forth are clarified.

In terms of the provisional means, the true reward land (*vipākabhūmi*), and the lands of humans and devas, the Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct Teachings are considered heterodox views; only the Perfect Teaching is truly correct.
Those who are not yet true men or women are all termed "those with heterodox views" prior to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. This is the exhortation for Bodhisattvas to uphold the name.
The "three many" and "four many" serve as the basis for comparison;
the sūtra cites sixty-two billion Ganges-sands as the standard, while regarding the currently dwelling bodhisattvas,
it cites four "few" to compare with the four "many."
The four [aspects] being many and the four [aspects] being few are equal in merit; this is the traditional fivefold explanation (including) the refutation [of other views].

According to the principle, the current explanation is unified: the first explanation concerns the equality of the phenomenon itself, while the second concerns the equality of the fact that the aspects of "many" and "one" are fused and identical in essence.
This is the *Dharmapada-śāstra*’s explanation of the meaning of "equality."
Contemplating the Correct Enlightenment (Appendix): The Second Round of Question and Answer Clarifying the Meaning of the Universal Gate,
wherein the merit of scattering a single flower into space by beggars and others toward the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha is not exhausted until one reaches Buddhahood.

Question: Regarding the meaning of the three karmas, the three benefits, the three non-guardings, the three absences of loss, and the three wheels of Avalokiteśvara—what is the intended meaning of the karma of body?
(Postscript) There are two meanings: (1) following oneself and following others; (2) having an object and lacking an object.
The Buddha’s response to the inquiry regarding the three karmas has two interpretations;
the thirty-three bodies and nineteen modes of teaching are condensed into ten realms.
The text omits the Bodhisattva realm; [this is followed by] four other interpretations (along with) the present interpretation.
The text omits the hell realm; [there are] three other interpretations (along with) the present interpretation that one possessing a hell-body preaches the Dharma (*pūrvaprayoga*).

Regarding the *Vāsava* anecdote, there is a general analysis by means of the four propositions concerning the ten bodies (*daśakāya*): (1) one body crossing one realm; (2) ten bodies crossing ten realms; (3) one body crossing ten realms; and (4) ten bodies crossing one realm.
The provisional means (*upāya*), the true reward (*vipākaphala*), and the *Avataṃsaka*’s perfect capacity: in one body, one realm is saved;
in the *Avataṃsaka*’s eight classes [of beings], through the separate and perfect [teachings], one Buddha saves one realm;
one realm saves many realms; many realms save one realm; and many realms save many realms.
The fourfold categorization (catuṣkoṭi) applied across the five flavors (pañcarasa) regarding the relative number of persons and dharmas;
the fourfold categorization regarding the relative number of causes and effects; the refutation of others' narrow and partial views;
the merging of the former thirty-three bodies into three categories; and the present school’s [treatment] as eight sections.
The scriptural passage concerning the Buddha-body manifested by Avalokiteśvara generally refers to the two bodies of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) and the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
The present text, however, specifically refers to the *sambhogakāya*.

Consequently, it is not realized that what is seen by the Perfectly Enlightened One of Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*) is likewise the sublime *sambhogakāya* within the *vipākaphala-kṣetra* (land of retributive fruition).
The Expedient Land (*upāya-bhūmi*) should be understood as having the meaning of a realm outside the [ordinary] world;
it is also termed the Land of Transformation (*pariṇāma-bhūmi*).
It has alternative names such as the Expedient Land and the Threefold Mind-made Body (*tri-vaśavarti-manomaya-kāya*), along with the fivefold and sevenfold [classifications].
The distinction between the superior and inferior responsive bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), the provisional and real recompense bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), and their respective lands;
the difference between the two types of responsive bodies and the combined body (*yuganaddhakāya*); and [Appendix] the meaning of the combined body according to the Shared Teaching (*p’unggyo*).

In the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*), there are two types of faculties—the sharp and the dull (Postscript). Regarding the three layers of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the Land of Expedient Means, the tenth stage of faith (*śraddhā*) destroys them.
As for the Land of Shared Residence of the Pure and the Impure, it receives the name "Shared Residence" because there are both pure and impure lands within it.
Regarding the purity and impurity of these lands, there are both horizontal and vertical dimensions.
The two lands, the Pure and the Impure, each possess both sharp and dull faculties, forming four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*):
practicing merit leads to birth in a light land; [the four permutations concerning] the three types of merit and the relative urgency or laxity of the vehicle and the precepts.
In the present world, there are two capacities, the great and the small;
therefore, the two responses—the Great and the Small—are distinguished by their similarities and differences in timing.
One should discern the characteristics of the sudden capacity as it is moved by the *Avataṃsaka*, the threefold illumination of the *Avataṃsaka*, and the five flavors of the *Nirvāṇa*.
Fascicle Four:
The Signs Manifested by Those of Lesser Capacities;
the Avataṃsaka Sūtra for those of lesser capacities is like being deaf and mute. (Entrusted Record), according to the meaning of the first division.
The third is the sign of gradual maturation: in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, those of the three vehicles all attain Buddhahood;
from beginning to end, they all enter the *tāmya* (ghee), the Buddha-wisdom, and *nirvāṇa*.
[Entrustment] Following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is taught.
The three types of *nirvāṇa*, the three kinds of cultivation,
the manifestation of various bodies, and the teaching of the perfect and gradual methods— these four points (as well as the Pure Land)— likewise apply to the distinct and perfect [teachings],
their fundamental contemplations, and their compassion.
Passing through various lands, encompassing both the provisional means (*upāya*) and the true reward (*vipāka*), one further perceives within the Sahā world two lands—
the provisional means and the true reward— which share the same name, "Dharmatā," yet differ in that the latter exists in the midst of space,
situated beneath the bodies of the Bodhisattvas.
The Sudden school possesses sharp faculties, while the Gradual school possesses dull faculties; within both the detailed Gradual and the Sudden, there are further distinctions of sharp and dull.
Pratyekabuddhas (the "Lower" section) are entrusted to Mañjuśrī for twenty-two trillion kalpas to act as Pratyekabuddhas;
Śrāvakas (the "Lower" section) are entrusted with the four types of withered and the four types of flourishing.
Regarding the six individuals and the Tathāgata adorning the twin trees to cross over the Buddha-realm:
this refers to the partial realization of those to be saved. The Buddhas whom they save must be those who have manifested as causal bodies;
their original state is low while their traces are high. Crossing from the first bhūmi up to Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) constitutes the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The white-colored samādhi beneath the body of the Brahmā King is neither grasped nor abandoned; (together with) the skillful means, it is the body of the Brahmā King and Śakra in the land of true recompense.
[Regarding] Īśvara (and) Maheśvara, [it is] entrusted to the various sūtras and śāstras;
[regarding] the Great General of Akaniṣṭha Heaven, there are various alternative theories concerning his being the body of a minor king; [this] also contains four propositions.
The Body of the Elder (Postscript): The ten virtues of the elder; the four assemblies of laymen, officials, brahmins, and bhikṣus;
and the body of women. (Postscript): The reason why the wives of minor kings are not explained.
The bodies of the boy and girl vidyās, the eight classes of beings (aṣṭabhūta),
and the four types of nāgas (annex): [these are] the nāgas,
devanāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras dwelling upon human houses.
The *garuḍa* (entrusted) gives gold-winged [offerings] and makes a pact with the *nāgas* (along with the four modes of birth);
they differ from the *kiṃnaras* (entrusted) regarding the meaning of "human and non-human";
the *mahoragas* (entrusted)—all eight classes transform their original forms to listen to the Dharma.
The Vajrapāṇi deity manifests his body from the lower realm into the higher realm;
as when a king hears of the quarreling ants, he gives a general reply to Śakra. (Attached: It should pervade all thirty-one [heavens].
In the *Avataṃsaka*, the text is extensive while the meaning is concise; in the present text, the text is concise while the meaning is extensive. (Attached:
The two rounds of question and answer regarding the "Destroyer of the Earth" each consist of three sections: general and specific exhortations to uphold [the teaching].
Some people take the general response to be a praise of virtues.
In the preceding and following questions and answers, there are two interpretations regarding the presence or absence [of the name] as granted by imperial decree;
the latent and manifest responses to the capacities [of beings] each possess both latent and manifest aspects.

Regarding the exhortation to make offerings below [the section on] "Chanting the Name of Avalokiteśvara Bestows Fearlessness," there are variant versions of the text concerning the jeweled necklaces (*ratnāvalī*).
The value is worth a hundred thousand taels of gold; this refers to the "explanation of the matter" (*shijie*) and the "explanation of contemplation" (*guanjie*).
The old commentary states this is a "repeated explanation of the gift of Dharma" (*zhong fashishi*);

the current commentary explains that it is like the "gift of material wealth" (*fashi cai*), which carries the same meaning as the "gift of Dharma. This concerns the matter of being unwilling to accept [the offering]; there are two interpretations for the contemplation.
Out of compassion for us, he divided the threefold explanation into two parts and offered them to the two Buddhas.
This indicates that the translator [Amoghavajra] and Master Zunshi have provided a complete structural outline (*kojie*) for the verses,
which consist of ten characters beginning with "Miaoxiang" (Wondrous Marks), each embodying two meanings.
"Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara":
this refers to the meaning of the three karmas—namely, hearing his name, seeing his body, and so forth—both in their hidden and manifest aspects;
"mindfully recollecting that Avalokiteśvara" refers to those two meanings.
Although it universally accommodates all capacities, its primary function is the perfect understanding; thus,
it returns to the original person,
for all difficulties are expressed through no more than the six elements of earth, water, and so forth.
The general purport of the benefits of sympathetic resonance is that the body and so forth, oppressed by immeasurable sufferings—
whether presented in prose or verse, collectively or individually, or in prior or subsequent sections—
are all designated as "evil realms" (durgati) when viewed from the perspective of the Buddha; this is further specifically demonstrated through the three karmas and nine realms.
The Five Contemplations, beginning with True Contemplation (Appendix): The character "guan" (contemplation) is pronounced with the departing tone;
compassion is termed "guan. The commentary clarifies two interpretations of the fundamental contemplation of compassion; this interpretation accords with the Buddha’s intent.
The light of wisdom shines universally,
able to subdue the calamitous winds and fires; the thunder of the precepts,
which are the essence of compassion, and the wondrous great cloud of a benevolent mind.
